metric_rationale: The experimental design was specifically crafted to dissociate Take The Best (TTB) from the Weighted Additive rule (WADD) by featuring trials where the most valid discriminating cue points to one option, but the sum of the remaining cues strongly favors the other option. This metric computes the proportion of choices that align with the TTB prediction across all trials. For data simulated under TTB, this metric will be very high (close to 1.0, minus lapse rate). For data simulated under WADD, the metric will be much lower (around 0.25), because WADD integrates all features and will therefore frequently oppose TTB's one-reason choices on this specific set of compensatory trial pairs. Because all subjects face the same balanced trial distribution, between-subject variance will be tight.

This metric computes the proportion of choices that align with the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic. The experimental design specifically pits TTB against WADD by creating compensatory trials where the single most valid discriminating cue points to one option, while the sum of all lower-validity cues points to the other. TTB will score very high on this metric (close to 1, limited only by noise), whereas WADD will score very low, effectively discriminating the two theories.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Tallying heuristic specifically on critical trials where Tallying and WADD make opposite predictions. On these trials, one option has 3 positive features with low validity, while the other has 2 positive features with high validity. Tallying will consistently prefer the option with 3 features (yielding a metric near 1.0), whereas WADD will strongly prefer the option with 2 high-validity features (yielding a metric near 0.0).

Trial 1 (A=[1,1,0,0,0], B=[0,0,1,1,1]) is the critical trial that dissociates the two models. Tallying relies purely on cue counts, evaluating B as superior (3 positive cues vs 2). WADD incorporates cue validities, recognizing that the first two cues are substantially more predictive than the last three, thus generally favoring A. By measuring the choice rate for Option A on this specific trial, we obtain a stark contrast: Tallying will yield a rate below 0.5, while WADD will yield a rate above 0.5.

This metric calculates the subject's accuracy on 'extreme' trials where one option completely dominates the other (i.e., has all positive features while the other has none). Under the Random Guessing theory, subjects ignore the stimulus, so their choice on these trials will only reflect their baseline bias, averaging to 0.5 across both types of extreme trials. Under the WADD theory, the large difference in weighted sums will lead to a very high probability of choosing the dominating option (bounded only by the lapse rate epsilon). Thus, WADD predicts a score significantly higher than 0.5, while Random Guessing predicts exactly 0.5.

Under the Weighted Additive (WADD) theory, subjects compute a weighted sum of features using the validities and choose the option with the higher score. Therefore, their choices will align with the higher WADD score significantly more often than chance. Under the Random Guessing theory, subjects ignore the features entirely, so the proportion of choices consistent with the WADD score will hover around 0.5. This metric directly calculates the accuracy of the deterministic WADD rule on trials with unequal scores, yielding a large and highly significant contrast between the two theories.
